paper.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

read_sources.note: Read for actor/evaluator/reflection framework, ALFWorld, HotPotQA, HumanEval/MBPP/LeetcodeHard results, ablations, and limitations.
Used for metadata, version history, abstract claims, and DOI.

summary.one_sentence: Reflexion teaches an LLM agent across trials by turning task feedback into verbal self-reflections stored in memory, without updating model weights.
summary.thesis: A natural-language critique can act as a semantic gradient: after a failed trajectory, the agent writes a lesson, stores it, and conditions the next attempt on that memory.
summary.why_it_matters: Reflexion makes agent learning a runtime data problem rather than only a training problem: trajectories, evaluator signals, reflections, and memory windows become first-class state.

prior_state: LLM agents could act in environments using prompting, but mostly learned from in-context examples rather than from their own failed trials.
Traditional reinforcement learning can learn from reward, but often requires many samples and expensive model updates.
Scalar rewards provide weak credit assignment for long language-agent trajectories.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks whether agents can improve over repeated attempts by converting feedback into natural-language experience summaries and reusing those summaries as memory.
assumptions: The task exposes some feedback signal, such as binary success, exact match, unit-test output, compiler logs, heuristics, or evaluator-model judgment.
The LLM can generate useful reflections from trajectory plus feedback.
The next trial can condition on a small memory of prior reflections within the context window.

concepts.name: Verbal reinforcement
concepts.definition: A reinforcement signal converted into natural-language feedback that guides future attempts.

concepts.name: Reflection memory
concepts.definition: A bounded episodic memory buffer of self-reflections generated after failed or completed trials.

concepts.name: Actor/evaluator/self-reflection loop
concepts.definition: A modular loop where an actor produces actions or code, an evaluator scores the result, and a reflection model writes lessons into memory.

method.core_idea: Run the agent for a task attempt, evaluate the trajectory, generate a natural-language reflection from the feedback and trajectory, append that reflection to memory, and retry with the memory in context until success or a trial limit.
action_grammar: Actor: the LLM policy that emits text, actions, or code conditioned on observations and memory.
Evaluator: an environment, heuristic, exact-match grader, test runner, compiler, or LLM that scores the trajectory.
Self-reflection: an LLM-generated verbal summary of the failure mode or lesson.
Memory: a bounded buffer of previous reflections, usually 1-3 experiences in the paper's setups.
steps: Generate an initial trajectory with an Actor such as ReAct or CoT.
Evaluate the result with task-specific feedback.
Ask the Self-Reflection model to convert feedback and trajectory into a useful lesson.
Retry the task with memory included in the Actor context until success, repeated failure, or max trials.
method.pseudocode:
memory = []
for trial in 1..max_trials:
    trajectory = actor(task, memory)
    reward, feedback = evaluator(trajectory)
    if reward == success:
        return trajectory
    reflection = reflect(trajectory, feedback, memory)
    memory = keep_recent(memory + [reflection], limit=3)
return failure

claims.statement: Reflexion reinforces an agent through verbal self-reflection stored in memory rather than through weight updates.
caveats: The method depends on the base model's ability to diagnose failures from feedback and trajectory context.

claims.statement: The framework decomposes learning into Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection, and memory components.
claims.scope: Section 3 modular formulation and Figure 2 algorithm.
caveats: The paper explores multiple evaluator types; choosing a reliable evaluator remains task-specific.

claims.statement: On ALFWorld, ReAct plus Reflexion solves far more tasks than ReAct alone over repeated trials.
claims.scope: 134 ALFWorld environments across six task types.
caveats: The setup uses a heuristic or LLM classifier to trigger reflection, resets the environment between trials, and truncates memory to the last three reflections.

claims.statement: On HotPotQA, Reflexion improves both CoT-style reasoning and ReAct-style retrieval/reasoning over repeated attempts.
claims.scope: 100 HotPotQA questions with exact-match feedback and memory size 3.
caveats: Exact match is a coarse binary reward for natural-language QA, and the CoT(GT) setup uses ground-truth context to isolate reasoning.

claims.statement: On coding tasks, Reflexion achieves the paper's headline 91% pass@1 on HumanEval and improves several Python/Rust code-generation benchmarks.
claims.scope: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval Rust, and LeetcodeHardGym experiments.
caveats: The paper notes MBPP Python underperforms GPT-4 baseline due to a high false-positive internal-test rate.

claims.statement: Reflexion can fail when feedback or self-tests are misleading, when memory is too small, or when verbal policy optimization gets stuck in a local minimum.
caveats: The paper explicitly prefers false negatives over false positives in code generation because false positives can prematurely accept wrong code.

evidence.result: The paper defines Reflexion as verbal reinforcement where an agent reflects on task feedback, stores reflective text in memory, and conditions future trials on that memory without updating LLM weights.

Reflexion uses an Actor to generate text/actions, an Evaluator to score trajectories, a Self-Reflection model to generate verbal cues, and short/long-term memory. The paper bounds reflection memory, usually to 1-3 stored experiences.

On 134 ALFWorld tasks, ReAct + Reflexion completes 130 of 134 tasks using the simple heuristic, and the paper summarizes an absolute 22% improvement over strong baselines in 12 iterative learning steps.
The paper reports Reflexion outperforms CoT-only, ReAct-only, and CoT(GT)-only baselines across several learning steps on 100 HotPotQA questions, and summarizes a 20% reasoning improvement.

The abstract reports 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, surpassing the previous GPT-4 80% baseline. Section 4.3 says Reflexion outperforms all baseline accuracies and sets new state-of-the-art standards on all Python/Rust benchmarks except MBPP Python.

The paper analyzes false positives/false negatives from generated unit tests, reports HumanEval Rust ablations where Reflexion with tests and self-reflection reaches 0.68 versus 0.60 baseline, and states Reflexion may get stuck in local minima while memory is limited to a sliding window.

agent_infra_takeaways: Reflexion makes failed trajectories reusable data. A runtime should persist trajectory, evaluator result, reflection text, and retry attempt together.
Feedback amplification is a separate component: scalar reward or binary failure is not enough unless converted into an actionable memory item.
Reflection memory needs lifecycle rules: size limits, replacement, retrieval, and stale or misleading lessons become correctness concerns.
External evaluators matter. Exact match, environment completion, compiler logs, and unit tests all create different reflection quality and failure modes.
For coding agents, generated tests are part of the trust boundary; false positives can make the agent accept wrong code.
caveats: Reflexion is not gradient-based reinforcement learning and does not update model weights.
The method depends on the LLM's self-evaluation or on task heuristics; poor feedback can produce poor reflections.
The memory window is small in the paper's experiments, usually 1-3 reflections, and can lose useful history.
Repeated retries increase cost and can still converge to non-optimal local behavior.
Code-generation success is bounded by the quality and coverage of generated tests or compiler feedback.

related_work.title: Self-Refine
related_work.note: The paper describes Self-Refine as effective for single-generation refinement, while Reflexion targets decision-making and persistent memory over trials.

poc.note: No PoC yet - contributions welcome. A useful local PoC would run a toy ReAct-like agent on deterministic text tasks, persist failed trajectories plus reflection notes, and compare first-attempt vs retry success.
